Existing empty furniture and the paper layout are moved under cover before the roof leak is detected. Covered is contrasted with dry: the leak makes a repair task necessary. Saturday09:00 cleaning,13:00 books at café,14:30 chairs at side entry and Sunday returns remain agreed, not completed.

All examples are translated. English sense cues live in exercise instructions, where RULES.md permits them; banks include at least3 same-class extra words and require unchanged encountered forms.

39 scheduled recalls occur in story roles: book ownership labels protect only the three actual books; chair-layout labels reveal that the attempted move crowds access; day/time words maintain the established appointments. grammar.title: Frase
grammar.rule: Amanhã vai chover. Nós vamos preparar o espaço. Os livros vão esperar aqui.
grammar.note_en:
This chapter adds ir + infinitive for a planned or expected future action. An infinitive is the verb’s naming form, such as preparar (“to prepare”), levar (“to carry”) or proteger (“to protect”). Put a present form of ir before it: vou, vai, vamos or vão, according to the subject. The second verb remains an infinitive. Vou levar o mapa means “I am going to take the map”; Você vai levar o mapa? means “Are you going to take the map?”; Nós vamos preparar o espaço means “We are going to prepare the space”; Os livros vão esperar aqui means “The books are going to wait here.” These are all expressions actually used in this chapter. They express future plans or expectations; English ‘going to’ does not require literal movement in either language.

The form of ir agrees with the subject. Eu uses vou; você, Rosa, Paulo, Ana, Bia, o vizinho and a vizinha each use vai. Nós uses vamos; they or plural subjects use vão. The table includes the subject/form pairings already demonstrated. Do not add an ending to the second verb: Ana e Bia vão limpar means “Ana and Bia are going to clean,” and Paulo vai ajudar means “Paulo is going to help.” The future construction does not grant an unseen full paradigm for another verb. Read each actual form in the story before producing it in a workbook block.

Compare the earlier movement meaning with the new construction. Ana e Bia vão ao pátio means “Ana and Bia go to the courtyard”: ao pátio names a destination. Não vão levar livros means “They are not going to take books”: levar is an infinitive and names the planned action. Negation goes before the form of ir. Os livros não vão estar fora agora means “The books are not going to be outside now”; Não vamos deixar os papéis fora do telhado means “We are not going to leave the papers outside the roofed area.” The story’s amanhã (“tomorrow”) helps identify a future situation, but it does not create the construction. Hoje (“today”) can also contain a plan for later today. The Friday visit and wet paper occur now; the roof work and cleaning are agreed for Saturday.

Portuguese weather expressions do not need an English-style dummy subject it. Chove means “It rains / It is raining.” In this weather use chover is impersonal: there is no person or plural subject controlling the action. Vai chover means “It is going to rain.” Keep singular vai in the ordinary impersonal weather frame; the number of people, books or chairs does not change it. Amanhã vai chover means “It is going to rain tomorrow.” In Chove hoje (“It is raining today”), the verb chove is a present statement, not the later estar + gerund progressive. This chapter introduces neither a gerund nor a conditional with se. The noun chuva, as in tem chuva (“there is rain”), is distinct from the verb chover. Sol means “sun”; vento means “wind”; céu means “sky”; água means “water.” The delivered meanings are anchored to this story’s sky, exposed papers and forecast, not an imported weather vocabulary list.

The new infinitives protect and change fit the same pattern. Nós vamos proteger os papéis means “We are going to protect the papers”; Vamos mudar o plano means “We are going to change the plan.” Proteger is the naming form; protege is the singular present in O telhado não protege a mesa (“The roof does not protect the table”). Mudar is the naming form; muda is the singular present in O plano das horas não muda (“The schedule does not change”). Cai is the present of cair in O papel de Ana cai no chão (“Ana’s sheet falls onto the floor”); Não pode cair perto da saída means “It must not fall near the exit.” The chapter uses only these encountered forms; no past or gerund of these verbs is taught.

The new adjectives describe conditions. O livro está molhado means “The book is wet”; a mesa está molhada, “the table is wet”; o mapa está seco, “the map is dry”; os papéis estão secos, “the papers are dry.” Wet and dry agree with the noun as shown in the table. Espaço coberto means “covered space”; telhado means “roof.” Coberto here is an adjective describing an area with a roof, not a lesson on passive voice or how to conjugate a verb meaning ‘cover.’ A covered place can still be wet if its roof lets water through; that distinction causes the change of plan.

Sem means “without” and takes a noun phrase here: sem telhado means “without a roof”; sem água, “without water”; sem saída, “without an exit.” Its contrast is the already known com (“with”). This chapter does not license sem + infinitive. Finally, a written plan is different from a completed action: the books are kept in the café cupboard, the two market deliveries keep Saturday13:00 and14:30, and no borrowed shipment arrives in this chapter. Saturday cleaning remains at nine in the morning. Agreement to work on the roof is the next practical task, not a claim that the roof is already sound.
